heading: The Manikya kings' independent kingdom
body: Tripura's history stands apart in India's northeast for how long it stayed continuously self-ruled. The Manikya dynasty governed the Twipra kingdom from the early 15th century, at times controlling a substantial stretch of the eastern subcontinent, making it one of the longest-ruling royal houses anywhere in South Asia. Unlike most of the surrounding hill regions, Tripura entered the colonial era not as annexed territory but as a princely state that negotiated its own terms with the British, coming under their paramountcy from 1809 while the Manikya kings retained internal rule.

That arrangement held through the end of British India. Tripura's ruler acceded to the newly independent Indian Union on 13 August 1947, but the kingdom itself continued to exist as a separate princely state for two more years, administered after the death of Maharaja Bir Bikram Kishore Manikya by a regency council under Maharani Kanchan Prabha Devi. A Merger Agreement was signed on 9 September 1949, and Tripura formally merged into the Indian Union on 15 October 1949 — ending, by negotiated agreement rather than conquest, more than five centuries of Manikya rule.
The places on this map sit inside that royal history: palaces, temples and sites built under the Manikya kings, and the transition points between an independent kingdom and a modern Indian state.
